This paper looks at how to generate more authentic emotional speech in conversations.
Conversational speech synthesis aims to make an agent's voice fit the current dialogue.
A key difficulty is that human emotions are much richer than a few fixed categories.
Another difficulty is the growing amount of redundant information in long dialogue histories.
To address both problems, the authors propose a framework called AuEmoChat.
First, AuEmoCodec learns discrete tokens that represent detailed emotional information.
Next, AuEmoToMe reduces redundant dialogue tokens while retaining useful emotion cues.
Finally, an emotion-aware flow-matching model converts these representations into expressive speech.
The experiments report improvements in both emotional expression and overall speech quality.
In ordinary text-to-speech, a sentence can often be synthesised without considering previous turns.
In a conversation, however, the same sentence may need very different emotional delivery.
Previous conversational systems have used acoustic features, graphs, and generative language models.
Some approaches also predict emotion labels or emotion descriptions before producing speech.
However, a label such as happiness covers many distinct states, including excitement and gentle pleasure.
A small emotion label space therefore limits how precisely a system can represent affect.
Meanwhile, multimodal dialogue histories become increasingly long as a conversation continues.
Many of these tokens add little useful information and may distract the context model.
The key research question is how to preserve subtle emotion while reducing unnecessary context.
AuEmoChat addresses this question through emotion tokenisation, context compression, and speech rendering.
Neural audio codecs are widely used to convert continuous speech into discrete units.
Most existing codecs focus on linguistic content, acoustic details, or speaker characteristics.
AuEmoCodec differs because its primary goal is to represent perceived emotion.
Traditional emotion systems often use a fixed collection of basic categories.
Fine-grained emotion modelling instead aims to capture mixtures and differences within these categories.
Token merging has also been studied as a way to reduce sequence length.
The distinctive idea here is to use emotion information to guide what should be merged.
The input contains previous speakers, dialogue text, speech signals, and emotion representations.
For the target turn, the system receives the speaker identity and the text to be spoken.
The first component is an emotion-focused neural codec called AuEmoCodec.
It uses finite scalar quantisation to learn a discrete emotion codebook.
The codebook contains one thousand possible positions, with about seven hundred and fifty used after training.
Unlike an ordinary audio codec, AuEmoCodec is not trained to reconstruct the original waveform.
Instead, it reconstructs perceived scores along seven basic emotion axes.
This encourages the learned tokens to retain subtle combinations of emotional states.
The second component is AuEmoToMe, a method for merging redundant context tokens.
It compares token representations to identify text and speech units that contain similar information.
Each utterance's emotion token acts as an anchor during the merging process.
This anchor helps the model retain context that matters for emotional prediction.
The compressed dialogue history is then passed to an autoregressive prediction model.
The model predicts the target emotion token together with the target speech tokens.
The final component generates a mel-spectrogram using conditional flow matching.
It combines the compressed context, the predicted emotion, and acoustic information.
An additional emotion classifier helps guide the generation towards the desired emotion.
This guidance is activated later in the flow process, when the acoustic representation is more stable.
A vocoder then converts the generated acoustic representation into audible speech.
The experiments use the NCSSD-EmCap conversational speech dataset.
This dataset combines DailyTalk, NCSSD, and MultiDialog.
It contains approximately three hundred and eighty-four hours of speech.
There are eighteen thousand five hundred and eighty dialogues and nearly two hundred and forty-six thousand utterances.
The experiments compare AuEmoChat with BaseCSS, ECSS, GPT-Talker, and Chain-Talker.
The authors also remove or vary individual components to study their contributions.
Naturalness DMOS asks listeners whether the generated speech sounds natural.
Emotion DMOS asks whether the expression fits the conversational context.
Word error rate measures whether the spoken words match the intended text.
Mel-cepstral distortion measures differences between acoustic features.
Speaker similarity evaluates whether the generated voice preserves the target speaker's identity.
The study also reports basic emotion accuracy and authentic emotion accuracy.
AuEmoChat achieves a naturalness DMOS of 4.171 in the reported comparison.
Its emotion DMOS reaches 3.979, above the compared baseline systems.
The reported word error rate is 9.14, while authentic emotion accuracy reaches 28.71.
The codec analysis favours finite scalar quantisation with a codebook size of one thousand.
A token merging rate of thirty per cent gives the strongest overall balance in the reported analysis.
Excessive token merging removes useful information and reduces performance.
These findings suggest that richer emotion representations and selective compression work well together.
The method still depends on the quality of the emotion supervision used to train the codec.
The authors propose extending the system to multilingual settings in future work.
They also aim to improve the interpretability and scale of authentic emotion modelling.
This paper focuses on emotional expressiveness in conversational speech synthesis.
The main goal is to generate speech with suitable prosody and emotional delivery.
Earlier work was limited by scarce emotional data and difficult emotion-state modelling.
The authors propose an emotional conversational speech synthesis system called ECSS.
The first module uses a heterogeneous graph to understand emotional dialogue context.
The second module uses an emotion renderer to infer the target speaking style.
The authors also enrich DailyTalk with emotion categories and emotion intensity labels.
The evaluation suggests that these components improve emotional speech generation.
A spoken dialogue system should react to both the meaning and the emotion of a conversation.
Conventional text-to-speech mainly determines speaking style from the target text or a reference.
Conversational speech synthesis also considers the interactions between speakers.
Earlier methods used recurrent models and graph networks to encode dialogue history.
These methods helped model speaker relationships and multimodal context.
However, they did not fully capture how emotion changes between dialogue turns.
The same target sentence can sound surprised, excited, or disappointed depending on the context.
The authors therefore treat emotion understanding as a core part of the synthesis problem.
They also argue that both emotion category and intensity should be represented.
The proposed system connects these sources of information through a heterogeneous graph.
Emotion recognition in dialogue has been studied using attention and graph-based models.
Some text-oriented methods focus mainly on linguistic meaning and emotion words.
Speech synthesis methods increasingly combine textual and acoustic dialogue information.
Earlier dialogue graphs often treated their nodes and relationships as homogeneous.
This is restrictive when text, speakers, acoustics, and emotion labels play different roles.
ECSS explicitly models these different information types within one emotional conversational graph.
The input history contains text, speaker identity, audio, emotion category, and emotion intensity.
For the target utterance, only the text and speaker are available.
The model must infer suitable emotional expression before producing the final speech.
The first step constructs an emotional conversational graph.
Different types of information become different types of graph nodes.
Graph relationships capture dependencies between the sources of conversational knowledge.
The graph nodes are initialised using modality-specific feature representations.
A heterogeneous graph transformer then exchanges information across node types.
This produces contextual features that reflect emotional developments in the dialogue.
The emotion renderer predicts the emotional state of the target sentence.
It also estimates emotion intensity and prosodic characteristics.
Contrastive learning encourages samples with similar emotional properties to have similar representations.
Samples with different emotional properties are pushed further apart.
The resulting context and prosody features condition the speech synthesiser.
The synthesiser is built around a FastSpeech 2 style acoustic architecture.
The main dataset is DailyTalk, which contains 2,541 dialogues.
It provides 23,773 audio clips and approximately twenty hours of speech.
The study adds seven emotion categories and three intensity levels to this dataset.
The data is divided into training, validation, and test subsets.
The authors compare their model with recurrent and homogeneous graph baselines.
Naturalness DMOS measures the perceived naturalness of the target speech.
Emotion DMOS evaluates emotional richness and consistency with dialogue history.
Mean absolute error is calculated for mel features, pitch, energy, and duration.
Lower acoustic prediction errors indicate more accurate reconstruction of the target features.
ECSS achieves a naturalness DMOS of 3.506 in its main comparison.
Its emotion DMOS reaches 3.619, above the recurrent and homogeneous graph baselines.
Removing emotion information reduces emotional speech performance.
Removing speaker or audio information also weakens the final synthesis quality.
Removing the contrastive objective causes a particularly clear reduction in emotion DMOS.
These results support the importance of joint context understanding and emotion rendering.
The approach requires useful emotion and intensity annotations for the historical dialogue.
The dataset is relatively small and contains only two recorded speakers.
A practical extension would be to model richer emotions with less annotation dependence.
This paper extends conversational speech synthesis to include visual responses.
Human communication uses facial expressions as well as spoken language.
Speech-only systems cannot fully reproduce these multimodal interactions.
The authors introduce conversational speech-visual synthesis as a new task.
They also present UniTalker, a unified model for multimodal understanding and generation.
The model predicts emotion, speech, and talking-face animations from dialogue context.
A landmark codec represents facial motion using compact discrete tokens.
A hard alignment strategy keeps speech and facial motion synchronised.
The reported results show gains in emotional consistency and visual naturalness.
Most earlier conversational speech systems respond to users only through audio.
These systems model linguistic content and speaking style from dialogue history.
However, face-to-face interaction also relies on eye contact and facial movement.
A digital human should ideally respond with coordinated speech and facial expressions.
Simply generating a talking face from completed speech can create mismatches.
A weak or ambiguous speech signal may lead to unstable facial animation.
Other methods may generate expressive video without precise control of facial landmarks.
The central challenge is to coordinate dialogue understanding, emotion, speech, and visual motion.
UniTalker therefore treats speech and facial expression as connected outputs of a single system.
Speech dialogue models have improved context understanding and emotional expression.
Talking-face models can animate portraits using acoustic input.
Some visual generation methods also use facial landmarks for greater motion control.
Neural codecs allow complex speech and visual signals to be represented as discrete tokens.
Directly tokenising full video frames can introduce substantial redundant content.
UniTalker instead focuses on compact facial landmark sequences.
The dialogue history includes speaker identity, text, speech, facial motion, and emotion.
The target turn provides the speaker and the text to be delivered.
The model must generate suitable speech and facial animation for that turn.
The first module converts dialogue information into unified token sequences.
Text and speaker information are represented alongside speech and visual features.
The face tokenizer uses a specialised codec named LmkCodec.
LmkCodec compresses facial landmark sequences into discrete representations.
It is designed to keep reconstruction quality high while controlling token length.
The speech and landmark token streams are organised at compatible frame rates.
This supports direct alignment between spoken content and lip motion.
An LLM-based module called EVSLM then models the complete dialogue context.
EVSLM first predicts the emotion needed for the target response.
It then generates the speech and visual tokens through coordinated sequence prediction.
The bimodal hard alignment strategy helps avoid duration mismatch between the outputs.
Emotion guidance further encourages consistency between the voice and facial expressions.
The speech renderer produces the audio signal from the predicted speech representation.
A talking-face renderer combines speech, facial landmarks, and a reference portrait.
The final output is a coordinated audiovisual response.
The study uses spoken dialogue, audiovisual dialogue, and single-utterance audiovisual datasets.
The spoken dialogue group includes DailyTalk and the English subset of NCSSD.
The audiovisual dialogue group is based on MultiDialog.
The single-utterance visual group includes RAVDESS, MEAD, and CelebV-HQ.
Training proceeds in stages, beginning with landmark codec training.
The system then uses speech pretraining and successive dialogue-based fine-tuning.
Speech naturalness and speech emotion are evaluated through listening tests.
Speaker similarity measures whether the synthesised voice matches the intended speaker.
Visual emotion accuracy checks whether the animation conveys the intended emotion.
Fréchet inception distance is used to assess aspects of visual generation quality.
Lip-sync metrics assess the correspondence between mouth movement and speech.
Subjective visual scores assess content alignment, naturalness, and expressiveness.
UniTalker generates speech that fits the dialogue and facial motion that follows the voice.
Its reported audiovisual results are stronger than the main compared conversational baselines.
Removing emotion guidance reduces speech and visual emotion consistency.
Removing the alignment strategy substantially damages lip synchronisation.
Removing dialogue history weakens both emotional understanding and final generation.
The landmark codec is an important factor in efficient and accurate visual modelling.
Joint audiovisual generation is more complex than conventional speech-only synthesis.
The framework also depends on suitable speech and facial motion training data.
Further work could explore real-time interaction and stronger generalisation to unseen situations.
This paper studies how to produce empathetic conversational speech.
The authors argue that context awareness alone does not guarantee genuine emotional understanding.
Some generative systems predict speech tokens without explaining the emotional decision.
These systems may also rely on speech codes containing redundant acoustic information.
To address these limitations, the paper proposes Chain-Talker.
The framework separates the task into emotion understanding, semantic understanding, and empathetic rendering.
It also introduces CSS-EmCap to create dialogue-aware emotional descriptions automatically.
The experiments suggest that step-by-step generation improves emotional appropriateness.
Empathetic conversational speech needs to match the user's feelings and the dialogue situation.
This requires both emotional understanding and expressive acoustic generation.
Earlier systems often focused on predicting speaking style from multimodal history.
Generative systems such as GPT-Talker instead predict discrete speech representations directly.
These methods improve naturalness but provide limited explanations of how emotions are inferred.
A direct speech-token prediction process does not explicitly describe the desired emotional state.
Many existing speech tokens also mix linguistic and acoustic information.
This mixture may make sequence modelling less efficient and harder to interpret.
The authors are inspired by systems that solve complex tasks through several stages.
They propose a chain that first explains the emotion and then models the speech content.
Chain-based reasoning breaks difficult tasks into a sequence of smaller decisions.
This strategy has appeared in dialogue generation and speech-language modelling.
Speech emotion captioning describes vocal emotion through natural language.
Manual emotional caption annotation is costly and difficult to scale.
Automatically generated captions may lack conversational awareness if they only use a few keywords.
Supervised semantic speech tokens can represent spoken content more directly than general acoustic codes.
The paper combines these ideas into a modular generation pipeline.
Chain-Talker receives previous dialogue turns together with the target text.
The history contains speaker information, speech, text, and emotional descriptions.
Different modalities are organised into a unified sequence for contextual modelling.
The framework uses a language-model component called EmGPT.
In the first stage, EmGPT predicts an empathetic caption for the target utterance.
The caption expresses the emotion and speaking style that fit the dialogue.
The second stage predicts a sequence of semantic speech tokens.
These tokens capture the content of the intended speech response.
The system uses supervised semantic tokenisation to reduce unnecessary acoustic redundancy.
The third stage synthesises the final audio from the predicted semantic tokens.
The predicted caption also guides how the emotional speech should be rendered.
This separation makes the emotional decision more explicit than direct speech-token generation.
The model is trained through a multi-stage learning strategy.
Early training develops speech generation ability before more detailed conversational modelling.
The paper introduces an automatic captioning pipeline called CSS-EmCap.
The pipeline extracts speech-related attributes at different levels.
Sentence-level features describe the style of individual utterances.
Dialogue-level information helps explain emotion in the wider conversational context.
An LLM uses these attributes to produce more detailed empathetic captions.
The process is applied to DailyTalk, NCSSD, and MultiDialog.
Together these datasets provide approximately three hundred and eighty-four hours of annotated speech.
The experiments examine whether chain-style generation can improve emotional speech in dialogue.
The evaluation includes comparisons with previous conversational synthesis systems.
The authors assess both the generated empathetic captions and the final speech.
They also conduct ablation studies to examine the roles of context, captions, and pretraining.
The main question is whether explicit emotional reasoning benefits the final acoustic output.
Caption quality is evaluated through human ratings and semantic similarity.
Caption diversity is also examined to avoid overly repetitive descriptions.
Naturalness DMOS evaluates how natural the generated speech sounds.
Emotion DMOS evaluates whether the response matches the emotional context.
Emotion classification accuracy measures how recognisable the intended emotion is.
Speaker similarity and alignment measures examine other aspects of synthesis quality.
Chain-Talker reports a naturalness DMOS of 4.147 on its main comparison.
Its emotion DMOS reaches 4.239, exceeding the compared GPT-Talker variants.
The CSS-EmCap caption evaluation also shows improvements over its comparison methods.
Removing dialogue context reduces both naturalness and emotional appropriateness.
Removing empathetic captions also causes a measurable performance drop.
Removing early pretraining produces an even larger reduction.
The study supports the value of separating emotional reasoning from speech token generation.
The quality of emotional captions affects the guidance available to the speech model.
The multi-stage pipeline also introduces additional components and training requirements.
An interesting research question is how robust these descriptions are in unfamiliar conversations.
This paper investigates emotion-aware conversational speech synthesis using a large language model.
Its main challenge is understanding emotional context from spoken conversation.
Emotionally appropriate speech depends on both what people say and how they sound.
The authors introduce a framework called JELLY.
JELLY combines speech emotion recognition with conversational context reasoning.
An emotion-aware Q-former connects acoustic emotion features to the language model.
Multiple partial LoRA modules adapt the model to different input modalities.
The system uses a three-stage learning pipeline to reduce the need for large emotional dialogue datasets.
The experiments show improved emotional context understanding and suitable speech generation.
Conventional speech synthesis can generate a sentence without modelling the earlier conversation.
Conversational speech synthesis must consider the relationship between current and previous turns.
Earlier methods used recurrent networks, graph encoders, and multimodal context models.
However, the same words can communicate different feelings through different voices.
Therefore, understanding spoken emotion is important for generating appropriate responses.
Existing approaches may rely on transcriptions or emotion labels during inference.
In realistic applications, these annotations may not be available.
Emotional conversational speech data is also relatively scarce.
JELLY aims to infer emotional context from speech using an LLM.
A central design choice is to connect recognised acoustic emotions with language-based reasoning.
GRU-based CSS methods use textual dialogue history to improve speaking style.
Multimodal graph models add information from earlier speech signals.
Contrastive CSS models improve the discriminability of context representations.
Emotion-aware CSS also explores predicting the emotion of a target utterance.
JELLY differs by using speech emotion perception and LLM reasoning within one pipeline.
The model first extracts speech representations through a Whisper encoder.
A time-and-layer-wise transformer selects features that are useful for recognising emotion.
The emotion-aware Q-former then uses learnable queries to collect emotion information.
A projection layer maps these features into the language model's representation space.
This makes it possible for the LLM to work with both emotion and text representations.
The model uses separate partial LoRA modules for emotional and textual inputs.
These adapters reduce the need to fine-tune every parameter of the language model.
In the first training stage, the model aligns speech emotions with textual descriptions.
This stage can use emotional speech datasets rather than full dialogue recordings.
In the second stage, the LLM learns to reason about emotion across dialogue turns.
Text-only dialogue data is used during pretraining to address data scarcity.
The framework then fine-tunes its emotion reasoning components on conversational speech.
The final learning stage connects the predicted emotion with the speech synthesis system.
At inference time, the system can derive emotional cues from speech rather than supplied emotion labels.
The study evaluates JELLY against standard and dialogue-aware speech synthesis systems.
The main comparison includes FastSpeech 2, a GRU-based model, and ECSS.
The authors also evaluate a speech-only configuration of JELLY.
This setting tests whether the framework can operate without externally supplied transcripts.
Naturalness DMOS and emotion DMOS are used for human listening evaluation.
Emotion classification accuracy measures agreement with the target emotion.
Word error rate and phoneme error rate measure intelligibility and content accuracy.
Pitch error and mel-cepstral distortion assess acoustic fidelity.
Duration and voiced-unvoiced metrics examine temporal and phonation properties.
JELLY achieves an emotion classification accuracy of 58.60 in its main comparison.
Its naturalness DMOS is 3.847, and its emotion DMOS is 3.987.
The reported results are stronger than the main comparison models on several emotional measures.
The speech-only variant also maintains useful emotion modelling ability.
These findings suggest that emotion recognition and language-based context reasoning can complement each other.
The three-stage system introduces additional training and integration complexity.
The approach relies on the quality of the speech emotion features extracted by its encoder.
A useful next question is how well its reasoning generalises to unfamiliar speakers and conversations.
This paper introduces a generative approach to expressive conversational speech synthesis.
The task is to synthesise a target response with a speaking style suited to the dialogue.
Earlier systems often used elaborate context encoders and small dialogue datasets.
The authors propose a model called GPT-Talker to simplify context modelling.
It converts multimodal dialogue history into a unified discrete token sequence.
A conversational GPT predicts the semantic and style tokens of the target response.
A conversational VITS model converts these predictions into expressive speech.
The paper also introduces NCSSD, a large natural conversational speech dataset.
The dataset contains English and Chinese recordings with a total duration of 236 hours.
The reported evaluation shows improvements in naturalness and expressiveness.
A conversational voice assistant must speak in a way that suits the interaction.
Earlier research improved speech style using recurrent context encoders and multimodal graphs.
Some methods use separate modules to model local and global contextual information.
These complex designs can require careful optimisation and additional engineering.
The authors argue that a language model may provide a more unified approach.
An autoregressive model can learn dependencies within a sequence of dialogue tokens.
However, ordinary conversational language models do not automatically produce expressive speech.
A speech-specific token representation and renderer are therefore needed.
Training data is another important challenge for generative conversational speech synthesis.
DailyTalk contains around twenty hours of recorded conversation and uses a relatively scripted style.
The authors therefore collect a larger dataset with more natural conversational expression.
Conversational language models increasingly process both speech and text.
Several spoken language models map acoustic signals into discrete units.
Other systems generate response text or predict emotion-related features.
GPT-Talker differs by predicting speech representations from a multimodal dialogue history.
Prior conversational synthesis systems also use recurrent networks and graph-based context models.
The paper aims to avoid the need for highly specialised context interaction modules.
GPT-Talker consists of two main components called ConGPT and ConVITS.
The first step tokenises both the text and the speech in dialogue history.
A phoneme encoder represents the text content.
An acoustic tokenizer converts speech into a sequence of discrete units.
The token stream is organised in the order of the conversation.
Text tokens and speech tokens are interleaved rather than grouped separately.
The resulting sequence gives ConGPT a unified description of the previous turns.
ConGPT predicts the target acoustic token sequence in an autoregressive manner.
These predicted units contain information about both meaning and speaking style.
ConVITS takes the target text and the predicted token representation as conditioning inputs.
Its content and token encoders combine linguistic content with context-dependent style.
A cross-attention mechanism integrates these representations for speech synthesis.
A separate timbre encoder allows the system to use a reference speaker's voice characteristics.
The final VITS synthesiser generates the waveform of the agent's response.
The model adopts staged training rather than learning all components from scratch at once.
This helps transfer basic speech generation ability before modelling expressive dialogue.
NCSSD stands for Natural Conversational Speech Synthesis Dataset.
It includes both naturally performed recordings and dialogue audio collected from television programmes.
The dataset covers English and Chinese speech.
Its total duration is approximately 236 hours.
The data supports training and evaluation of generative dialogue-aware speech systems.
The authors evaluate GPT-Talker on DailyTalk and their newly collected NCSSD.
The comparisons include conversational speech synthesis methods with alternative context models.
The study examines perceived naturalness, emotional delivery, and speaker consistency.
It also analyses the contribution of the staged training strategy.
Further experiments investigate how the amount of dialogue context affects synthesis.
Naturalness DMOS evaluates the overall perceived quality of generated speech.
Emotion DMOS evaluates whether speech expression suits its dialogue context.
Speaker similarity evaluates how closely the synthesised voice matches the reference speaker.
Dynamic time warping distance is used to compare pitch-related expressive patterns.
The study also uses preference tests to assess the quality of NCSSD-based synthesis.
On DailyTalk, GPT-Talker reports a naturalness DMOS of 3.890.
Its emotion DMOS reaches 3.908 in the same comparison.
These scores exceed those of the compared context modelling baselines.
The results on the English NCSSD subset show a similar overall pattern.
The staged training analysis supports gradual adaptation to conversational expression.
The study also shows that changing dialogue length beyond the trained setting can hurt performance.
This observation highlights a challenge in modelling longer dialogue histories.
The pretrained model has difficulty when the inference context becomes longer than expected.
The speech tokens may still contain redundant information unrelated to the target emotion.
A natural future direction is to improve long-context modelling and control over speaking style.
This paper explores retrieval-augmented generation for conversational speech synthesis.
Conventional systems mainly use the current dialogue history to predict speaking style.
However, earlier stored dialogues may contain useful examples of similar conversational situations.
The authors propose a framework called RADKA-CSS.
It first retrieves stored dialogues that are similar in both meaning and style.
It then models current and retrieved dialogues using multi-granularity heterogeneous graphs.
A knowledge aggregation module combines the retrieved style information with the current context.
The aggregated representation is used to generate expressive speech.
The reported experiments show improvements in naturalness and style consistency.
A dialogue contains useful information about how the next sentence should sound.
Most conversational speech synthesis systems focus on the immediately available history.
However, previous interactions can preserve examples of similar topics, situations, and speaking styles.
This stored dialogue knowledge can support more appropriate speech generation.
Retrieval-augmented generation already uses external information to improve other generation tasks.
The paper asks whether similar ideas can improve spoken expression.
A suitable retriever must consider not only the topic but also the style of a dialogue.
Retrieved examples must then be represented in a form that supports synthesis.
The authors address these challenges with semantic-style retrieval and graph-based fusion.
Retrieval-augmented generation is widely used to connect a generative model with stored knowledge.
Most dialogue RAG applications focus on retrieving text to improve textual answers.
RADKA-CSS instead retrieves dialogue examples to improve speech style.
Contrastive learning can improve the separation of relevant and irrelevant representations.
Graph models can represent relations among utterances, words, and dialogue-level features.
The paper combines retrieval, contrastive learning, and multi-granularity graph modelling.
The framework distinguishes the current dialogue from stored dialogue history.
The first step builds a semantic-style database of stored dialogues.
Each entry contains dialogue text and audio together with their learned representations.
A multi-attribute retriever compares the current dialogue with the stored examples.
It considers semantic similarity and speaking-style similarity at the dialogue level.
The retriever selects the top-ranked dialogue examples for further processing.
The next step represents the dialogues using heterogeneous graphs.
The graphs contain word-level, sentence-level, and dialogue-level nodes.
Relationships connect information at different scales and across neighbouring turns.
Separate text and acoustic graphs capture semantic and style characteristics.
Graph encoders aggregate neighbouring information into richer dialogue representations.
The current dialogue is encoded using the same multi-granularity modelling approach.
A retrieval-based contrastive objective improves semantic and style discrimination.
Positive dialogue pairs are encouraged to have similar representations.
Irrelevant dialogues are pushed away in the learned representation space.
The knowledge aggregation module weights retrieved styles according to semantic relevance.
It combines retrieved style features with the current dialogue and predicted target style.
The fused information is finally supplied to the speech synthesiser.
The main experiments are conducted on the DailyTalk benchmark dataset.
The authors construct a stored dialogue database for semantic and style retrieval.
Comparison systems include DailyTalk, M2-CTTS, CONCSS, and ECSS.
The ablation study removes retrieval knowledge, graph structures, and aggregation components.
The authors also examine the effect of providing better retrieved examples.
Naturalness DMOS asks whether the generated voice sounds natural in conversation.
Style DMOS asks whether the voice matches the style of the current dialogue.
Comparative MOS evaluates preferences between two systems.
Pitch, energy, and duration errors are measured using mean absolute error.
Retrieval quality is also examined using a recall-based evaluation.
RADKA-CSS reports a naturalness DMOS of 3.904 in its main study.
Its style DMOS reaches 3.879, above the main comparison models.
The model also reduces the reported pitch, energy, and duration prediction errors.
Removing retrieved stored-dialogue knowledge leads to lower synthesis scores.
Replacing the multi-granularity graph with simpler structures also reduces performance.
The contrastive objective contributes to the quality of the learned dialogue representations.
Using more accurate retrieved examples produces additional improvements.
These results highlight the importance of retrieval quality and knowledge fusion.
The system depends on the availability of a useful stored dialogue database.
Incorrect retrieval may introduce an unsuitable speaking style into the synthesis process.
Improving dialogue retrieval and reducing retrieval cost are meaningful directions for future study.
This paper studies how multimodal dialogue context influences the prosody of a new utterance.
Both text and speech contain useful but different contextual information.
Earlier systems did not explicitly model all interactions between the history and target modalities.
The authors propose a framework called I-three-CSS.
It models both intra-modal and inter-modal interactions.
Four interaction paths link historical text or speech with target text or speech.
Contrastive learning strengthens these contextual relationships during training.
The study reports improved conversational prosody on DailyTalk.
Conversational speech synthesis should produce speech with contextually appropriate prosody.
This is important for voice assistants and other interactive systems.
Textual dialogue history provides semantic information about the conversation.
Acoustic history provides cues about speaking style and vocal expression.
These two sources can influence the next utterance in different ways.
Existing approaches often encode the history without explicitly relating it to the target modalities.
The authors argue that intra-modal and cross-modal interactions should be studied separately.
Their objective is to learn more reliable semantic and prosodic contextual features.
Recurrent models are often used to summarise text-based dialogue history.
Multimodal context encoders combine text and speech representations.
Graph-based systems capture relationships between speakers and dialogue turns.
Contrastive learning can enhance the distinction between different dialogue contexts.
The key difference in this paper is the explicit interaction between historical and target modalities.
The proposed model contains intra-modal modules, inter-modal modules, a text encoder, and a synthesiser.
The first intra-modal path links historical text with the next text.
This path is designed to capture semantic continuity across dialogue turns.
The second intra-modal path links historical speech with the next speech.
This path models the continuation of prosodic patterns in the conversation.
The first inter-modal path links historical text with the next speech.
It learns how earlier linguistic content can influence the next utterance's prosody.
The second inter-modal path links historical speech with the next text.
It helps the model capture information that complements the target sentence's semantics.
Historical text is encoded with pretrained semantic representations and a recurrent context model.
Historical speech is encoded with acoustic features and temporal modelling.
Attention mechanisms combine information across neighbouring turns.
Contrastive objectives align relevant historical representations with the target modalities.
The four learned interaction features are combined with the target text encoding.
During inference, target speech is not available, so the system uses learned historical interactions.
The speech synthesiser produces a waveform with dialogue-appropriate prosodic characteristics.
The experiments use DailyTalk, an English spoken dialogue dataset.
It contains 2,541 dialogues and 23,773 audio segments.
The total recording duration is approximately twenty hours.
The study compares the proposed model with recurrent, graph-based, and contrastive baselines.
Ablation experiments examine the four interaction paths individually and together.
Naturalness DMOS measures the perceived naturalness of the synthesised voice.
Prosody DMOS measures how well intonation and rhythm fit the dialogue.
Pitch mean absolute error measures the accuracy of pitch prediction.
Energy and duration errors measure other aspects of acoustic prosody.
I-three-CSS reaches a naturalness DMOS of 3.864 in its ablation table.
Its prosody DMOS reaches 3.876 in the same evaluation.
Combining all four interaction modules gives stronger performance than using isolated paths.
Removing the interaction enhancement mechanism reduces both subjective scores.
The acoustic prediction errors are also lowest in the full configuration of this comparison.
This supports the value of modelling historical and target modalities jointly.
The model uses separate pathways, which can increase architectural complexity.
The evaluation is mainly based on one relatively small English dialogue dataset.
A useful next step is to test whether the same interactions help larger generative models.
This paper investigates fine-grained interactions in conversational speech synthesis.
Earlier methods mainly model interactions at the utterance level.
However, words within a dialogue contain detailed semantic and prosodic information.
The authors argue that these word-level interactions deserve explicit modelling.
They propose a model called MFCIG-CSS.
The model constructs a semantic interaction graph and a prosody interaction graph.
Both graphs represent how word-level information influences later utterances.
The resulting features guide a speech synthesiser to produce more appropriate prosody.
Experiments on DailyTalk show improvements over the compared systems.
Conversational speech generation must consider what happened in previous turns.
Dialogue history contains both textual semantics and acoustic expressions.
A sentence-level representation can capture broad conversational dependencies.
However, it may miss important differences between individual words.
A particular word may carry emphasis, surprise, or another prosodic cue.
These details may affect the way the next speaker should respond.
The authors therefore study interactions between word-level content and later utterance-level states.
They separate semantic interaction from prosodic interaction.
This separation allows the model to learn complementary contextual information.
Earlier CSS approaches have used recurrent networks to represent dialogue history.
Other systems employ graph neural networks for speaker and utterance interactions.
Recent models also study interactions between historical and target modalities.
However, many of these relations are represented at the sentence or utterance level.
MFCIG-CSS extends the analysis to word-level semantic and acoustic information.
MFCIG-CSS has three main components.
They are a semantic interaction graph, a prosody interaction graph, and a speech synthesiser.
The semantic interaction graph is abbreviated as SIG.
SIG combines utterance-level semantic nodes with word-level text and acoustic nodes.
The graph represents how earlier words can influence later sentence meaning.
Text encoders extract semantic features from the dialogue content.
Acoustic encoders extract word-level prosodic information from aligned speech.
Graph convolution operations exchange information across these node types.
A final semantic interaction representation summarises the information from the graph.
The second graph is called the prosody interaction graph, or PIG.
PIG has a related structure, but its main path follows acoustic prosodic changes.
It models how word meaning and word prosody affect subsequent utterance prosody.
A dedicated interaction node collects the final prosodic representation.
The semantic and prosody features are fused with the target text representation.
The synthesiser then generates speech conditioned on these fine-grained interactions.
The acoustic generation architecture follows the earlier I-three-CSS setup.
The main experiments are performed on DailyTalk.
The study compares MFCIG-CSS with several representative conversational synthesis methods.
These include CONCSS, ECSS, and I-three-CSS.
Ablation experiments separately remove the semantic and prosody interaction graphs.
This allows the authors to evaluate the contribution of each pathway.
Naturalness DMOS measures whether the audio sounds natural to listeners.
Prosody DMOS measures whether the speech expresses appropriate conversational intonation.
Pitch mean absolute error evaluates the accuracy of the pitch pattern.
Energy mean absolute error measures the prediction of acoustic energy.
Mel-cepstral distortion measures differences in spectral characteristics.
The full model reports stronger subjective prosody scores than the main comparison systems.
The results support the value of word-level interaction modelling.
Removing the semantic graph reduces the quality of context-dependent speech generation.
Removing the prosody graph also reduces performance on prosody-related measures.
Removing both interaction graphs produces a particularly large decline.
The study suggests that semantic and prosodic interactions provide complementary information.
The authors evaluate the graph modules using a FastSpeech 2 based architecture.
They have not yet extended the framework to all token-based speech generation architectures.
The current graphs do not explicitly include all acoustic phenomena, such as pauses and emphasis.
Future work aims to add these richer prosodic details and study broader synthesis models.
This paper explores contrastive learning for conversational speech synthesis.
The goal is to generate speech with prosody that fits the previous dialogue.
Earlier context encoders sometimes failed to distinguish between different conversational situations.
The authors propose a model called CONCSS.
The model learns more discriminative dialogue representations through a self-supervised pretext task.
A hard negative sampling strategy makes context learning more challenging.
An autoregressive prosody module further improves the generation of natural intonation.
The evaluation shows improvements in context-sensitive prosody.
Modern text-to-speech systems can produce high-quality audio.
However, realistic dialogue requires more than clear pronunciation.
The voice must react appropriately to the speaker's previous context.
Multimodal dialogue history can provide linguistic and acoustic clues.
Existing context encoders may not distinguish subtle changes between dialogue situations.
A stronger context representation should respond to meaningful changes in historical speech.
Contrastive learning offers a way to separate different contexts in the representation space.
The authors therefore design a context-specific pretext task for conversational synthesis.
They also consider how to choose negative samples that are difficult to distinguish.
Early conversational speech synthesis used recurrent encoders to model previous utterances.
Multimodal models combine text and acoustic history to predict speaking style.
Contrastive learning is often used to improve representation quality without explicit class labels.
Triplet learning compares an anchor with one positive and one negative example.
CONCSS adapts these principles to context representations for speech synthesis.
The first step extracts textual and acoustic representations of the dialogue history.
A context encoder summarises each modality into a representation vector.
The pretext task defines positive and negative dialogue examples.
A positive example comes from the same dialogue with a different history length.
A negative example comes from another dialogue with a different context.
The model is trained to make positive representations more similar.
It also separates the anchor representation from negative contexts.
Some negative samples come from different conversations involving the same speakers.
These same-speaker negatives can be difficult because their speaking characteristics are similar.
Other negative examples come from conversations with different speakers.
A triplet loss encourages a useful margin between positive and negative samples.
The constraint is applied to both textual and acoustic context features.
The learned context embeddings are then used to condition speech generation.
An autoregressive prosody module models dependencies between neighbouring prosodic states.
It uses a pretrained prosodic language model to encourage fluent expression.
The overall architecture extends a VITS-based speech synthesis backbone.
The study uses a Chinese conversational speech corpus for model training.
The speech synthesis backbone is first pretrained on the Biaobei Chinese dataset.
The authors compare the framework with GRU-based synthesis and M2CTTS.
They also test alternative contrastive objectives and negative sampling strategies.
The effect of autoregressive prosodic modelling is evaluated separately.
Naturalness MOS rates the overall naturalness of the synthesised speech.
Comparative MOS asks listeners which of two systems has more suitable conversational prosody.
Mel loss measures the difference between predicted and reference acoustic spectra.
Log pitch root mean squared error measures errors in fundamental frequency patterns.
Mel-cepstral distortion measures spectral differences after alignment.
The full CONCSS system reports a naturalness MOS of 3.967.
It outperforms the main recurrent and multimodal comparison systems in the reported evaluations.
The triplet loss improves contextual discrimination compared with simpler contrastive learning.
Hard negative sampling provides a further improvement in contextual prosody.
The autoregressive prosody module also improves naturalness scores.
The results show that better context embeddings can lead to more suitable speech prosody.
The quality of the learned representation depends on how positive and negative examples are selected.
Some same-speaker negatives may be challenging but not equally informative.
Future research could study more adaptive sampling and richer dialogue context representations.
